rows.speaker: الفضل بن عيسى بن أخي الرقاشي
rows.claim: Israelites demanded that Moses prove his claim by letting them see God openly; God then ordered him to select seventy for the appointed meeting.
rows.anchor: عن الفضل بن عيسى بن أخي الرقاشي أن بني إسرائيل قالوا ذات يوم لموسى عليه السلام ألست ابن عمنا ومنا وتزعم أنك كلمت رب العزة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The account implies this was not the first appointed meeting; al-Suddi and al-Hasan also allow that the meeting was a different one, so al-Suddi is not alone.
rows.anchor: ظاهر في أن هذا الميقات ليس هو الأول نعم إنه مخالف لما روي عن السدي لكنهما متفقان على القول بالغيرية ويوافق السدي في ذلك الحسن أيضا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alusi rejects the claim that al-Suddi's account conflicts with what Muhyi al-Sunna transmitted.
rows.anchor: وما ذكره من مخالفة كلام السدي لما نقله محيي السنة في حيز المنع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some exegetes plausibly say Moses selected the seventy twice.
rows.anchor: والقول بأن الإختيار كان مرتين غير بعيد وبه قال بعضهم

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: In al-Suddi's account, after the calf episode and repentance, God ordered Moses to bring Israelites to apologize for calf worship and then choose seventy, favoring the first branch of al-Qutb's proposed alternatives.
rows.anchor: انطلق موسى إلى ربه فكلمه فلما كلمه قال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The demand to apologize after repentance could seek greater divine approval and mercy, emphasize the crime's enormity and need for further pardon, or have preceded the self-killing; their later realization of its gravity explains the order.
rows.anchor: والقول بأنه لا معنى للاعتذار بعد قتل أنفسهم ونزول التوبة أجيب عنه بأن المعنى يحتمل أن يكون طلبا لزيادة الرضى واستنزال مزيد الرحمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The seizure may have been a thunderbolt or the mountain's quake; most say all seventy died and God revived them, while others say they fainted and recovered, for their demand to see God, to show God's majesty, or as discipline.
rows.anchor: أي الصاعقة أو رجفة الجبل فصعقوا منها والكثير على أنهم ماتوا جميعا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Israelites' demand to see God was apparently made at the meeting place, not after their return; this makes it unlikely to be Moses' first meeting, since his request for vision followed God's speech without a break.
rows.anchor: لن نؤمن الخ صدر منهم في ذلك المكان لا بعد الرجوع كما قيل

rows.speaker: علي
rows.claim: Ali reports that, after Aaron died, Israelites accused Moses of killing him; seventy were chosen, asked to become prophets, were seized, and returned revived as prophets.
rows.anchor: لما حضر أجل هارون أوحى الله تعالى إلى موسى عليه السلام أن انطلق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alusi considers Ali's account unlikely to be sound because reports converge against it and the verses' apparent meaning resists it.
rows.anchor: لايكاد يصح فيما أرى لتظافر الآثار بخلافه وإباء ظواهر الآيات عنه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses' appeal that God could have destroyed them earlier recalls God's prior mercy in sparing them, including from Pharaoh and drowning, and seeks renewed mercy.
rows.anchor: عرض للعفو السابق لاستجلاب العفو اللاحق يعني أنك قدرت على إهلاكهم قبل ذلك بحمل فرعون على إهلاكهم وبإغراقهم في البحر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other explanations of “before” place it when they failed to stop calf worship, when Moses requested vision, or when he killed the Egyptian; another says he wished all to perish rather than witness their disobedience, which Alusi finds doubtful.
rows.anchor: حين فرطوا في النهي عن عبادة العجل وما فارقوا عبدته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses' inclusion of himself is humility and submission; he may mean that God could have destroyed him too when he requested vision or killed the Egyptian.
rows.anchor: تسليما منه وتواضعا وقيل : أراد بقوله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The question about destroying them for the fools' deeds refers either to obstinacy and bad manners or to calf worship; its interrogative can deny destruction in confidence in divine kindness, as Ibn al-Anbari says, or plead for mercy, as al-Mubarrad says.
rows.anchor: من العناد وسوء الأدب أو من عبادة العجل والهمزة إما لإنكار وقوع الإهلاك ثقة بلطف الله عزوجل كما قال ابن الأنباري أو للاستعطاف كما قال المبرد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alusi rejects assigning the plea to one of the seventy; the objection that its irritation would not suit prophecy is unpersuasive, since Moses may be voicing the afflicted group's plea.
rows.anchor: كان ذلك قالة بعضهم غير ظاهر ولا داعي إليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The statement that the trial was God's trial resumes and explains what preceded, excusing the people: God tested them by letting them hear His speech or by causing the calf to moo, so they misapplied an analogy and strayed.
rows.anchor: استئناف مقرر لما قبله وإعتذار عما وقع منهم

rows.speaker: راشد بن سعد
rows.claim: A report says Moses asked who put spirit into the calf; God answered that He did, and explained that He saw the people's inclination in their hearts and made the calf's effect easy for them.
rows.anchor: أخرج ابن أبي حاتم عن راشد بن سعد أن الله تعالى لما قال لموسى عليه السلام إن قومك اتخذوا عجلا جسدا له خوار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alusi suggests the report may allude to an eternal predisposition that was not itself created.
rows.anchor: ولعل هذا إشارة إلى الإستعداد الأزلي الغير المجعول

rows.speaker: الربيع وابن جبير وأبو العالية
rows.claim: These authorities take the pronoun in “it is only Your trial” to refer to the quake, meaning the hardship of enduring God's imposed worship and trial.
rows.anchor: الضمير راجع على الرجفة أي ما هي إلا تشديدك التعبد والتكلف علينا بالصبر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another interpretation makes the pronoun refer to Moses' request to see God, although that request was not stated in this immediate passage.
rows.anchor: الضمير لمسئلة الإراءة وإن لم تذكر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The next clause may explain the trial or function as a circumstantial clause; it means God misguides through overstepping or following illusions and guides by strengthening faith.
rows.anchor: استئناف مبين لحكم الفتنة وقيل : حال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other readings of the clause say the quake strikes whomever God wills and is diverted from whomever He wills, or that patience and acceptance earn reward and Paradise while rejecting the trial forfeits them; Alusi finds this latter account weak.
rows.anchor: المعنى تصيب بهذه الرجفة من تشاء وتصرفها عمن تشاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling God their protector means He alone manages their worldly and afterlife affairs; Moses asks forgiveness for what would incur punishment and mercy through worldly and afterlife blessings.
rows.anchor: أي أنت القائم بإمورنا الدنيوية والآخروية لا غيرك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The connective makes the plea follow from God's guardianship, which entails averting harm and bringing benefit; forgiveness precedes mercy because removing wrong comes before adorning with good, and Moses may include himself in the plea.
rows.anchor: والفاء لترتيب الدعاء على ماقبله من الولاية لأن من شأن من يلي الأمور ويقوم بها دفع الضر وجلب النفع وقدم طلب المغفرة على طلب الرحمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alusi rejects the claim that Moses sought forgiveness for the boldness of calling the trial God's, since the flow does not suggest God counted it as a sin.
rows.anchor: جرأة عظيمة فطلب من الله تعالى غفرانها والتجاوز عنها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some interpret the ending as erasing a wrong and replacing it with a good deed, so it closes both the plea for forgiveness and for mercy.
rows.anchor: وفسر بعضهم ماذكر بغفران السيئة وتبديلها بالحسنة ليكون تذييلا لاغفر وارحم معا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God is the best forgiver because others forgive for self-serving motives, while He forgives solely from grace; the closing statement reinforces the plea, and forgiveness is singled out as most important.
rows.anchor: إذ كل غافر سواك إنما يغفر لغرض نفساني

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Write for us” means establish or allot for us a good in this worldly life: a pleasant life and success in obedience.
rows.anchor: واكتب لنا أي ثبت وأقسم لنا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some take the worldly good to mean favorable praise, but Alusi says this is not a good interpretation.
rows.anchor: وقيل : ثناءا جميلا وليس بجميل

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says the worldly good is forgiveness and mercy before Moses and his people depart.
rows.anchor: وعن ابن عباس رضي الله تعالى عنهما أن المراد قبل وفادتنا وردنا بالمغفرة والرحمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The requested good in the afterlife is the best reward and the Garden.
rows.anchor: أي واكتب لنا أيضا في الآخرة حسنة وهي المثوبة الحسنى والجنة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some read the afterlife request as a restatement of “forgive and have mercy on us.”
rows.anchor: إن هذا كالتأكيد لقوله : إغفر وارحم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “We have turned to You” means we repented and returned to God, from the verb for returning and repenting.
rows.anchor: إنا هدنا إليك ( أي تبنا إليك من هاد يهود

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alusi cites an anonymous line of poetry as evidence for the sense of returning or repenting: “I am one who turns back from what I have done.”
rows.anchor: قال : إني امرىء مما جنيت هائد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An anonymous expression, “O rider of sin, bow down and prostrate,” is cited in discussing the verb's usage.
rows.anchor: ياراكب الذنب هدهد واسجد كأنك هدهد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another gloss takes “hudnā” to mean that the people inclined or turned toward God.
rows.anchor: معناه مال وقرأ زيد بن علي

rows.speaker: زيد بن علي
rows.claim: Zayd ibn Ali reads the word with kasra on the hāʾ, deriving it from a verb meaning to move or incline.
rows.anchor: وقرأ زيد بن علي رضي الله تعالى عنهما ( هدنا ) بكسر الهاء

rows.speaker: أبو وجرة السعدي
rows.claim: Abu Wajrah rejects the damma reading as unknown in Arabic and says only the kasra form meaning “we inclined” is used; Alusi says mass transmission refutes him.
rows.anchor: وأخرج ابن المنذر وغيره عن أبي وجرة السعدي أنه أنكر الضم وقال : والله لاأعلمه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: With the kasra reading, the verb may be active or passive, meaning either “we moved ourselves” or “we moved others”; both voices are also allowed on the common reading in a dialectal usage.
rows.anchor: وجوز على هذه القراءة أن يكون الفعل مبنيا للفاعل والمفعول بمعنى حركنا أنفسنا أو حركنا غيرنا وكذا على قراءة الجماعة

rows.speaker: السمين
rows.claim: Al-Samin objects to al-Zamakhshari's allowance of both voices: when the form is ambiguous, a vowel should distinguish them; Alusi notes Sibawayh allowed all three forms for “qīla” without qualification.
rows.anchor: وتعقبه السمين بأنه متى حصل الإلتباس وجب أن يؤتي بحركة تزيله

rows.speaker: سيبويه
rows.claim: Sibawayh allows the three vocalizations in forms such as “qīla” without qualification.
rows.anchor: إلا أن سيبويه جوز في نحو قيل الأوجه الثلاثة من غير إحتراز

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The repentance clause explains the plea for forgiveness and mercy; the emphatic particle in “we have turned” displays eagerness for its substance.
rows.anchor: والجملة تعليل لطلب المغفرة والرحمة وتصديرها بحرف التحقيق لأظهار كمال النشاط والرغبة في مضمونها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “He said” begins an explanatory resumption; God's punishment reaches whomever He wills to punish, with no outside party determining it.
rows.anchor: إستئناف بياني كأنه قيل : فماذا قال الله تعالى له بعد دعائه

rows.speaker: الحسن وعمرو الأسود
rows.claim: Al-Hasan and Amr al-Aswad read “whoever does evil” with sīn rather than “whoever I will”; the reading is also attributed to Zayd ibn Ali, though some deny its authenticity.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الحسن وعمرو الأسود ( من أساء ) بالسين المهملة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's mercy encompasses everything: every person, believer or unbeliever, obedient or sinful, enjoys divine blessings in this life.
rows.anchor: أي شأنها أنها واسعة تبلغ كل شيء ما من مسلم ولا كافر ولا مطيع ولا عاص إلا وهو متقلب في الدنيا بنعمتي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The shift from present-tense punishment to past-tense mercy suggests mercy is intrinsic while punishment arises from people's sins; divine will also applies to mercy, though it is not stated explicitly.
rows.anchor: وفي نسبة الإصابة إلى العذاب بصيغة المضارع ونسبة السعة إلى الرحمة بصيغة الماضي إيذان بأن الرحمة مقتضى الذات وأما العذاب فمقتضى معاصي العباد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God will specifically inscribe mercy for those who fear disbelief and sins, whether from the outset or after falling into them, and who pay the zakat required of them.
rows.anchor: أي الكفر والمعاصي إما إبتداءا أو بعد الملابسة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A reported gloss takes piety to mean obeying God and His Messenger, but Alusi says the apparent sense is otherwise.
rows.anchor: وقيل المعنى يطيعون الله ورسوله صلى الله تعالى عليه وسلم والظاهر خلافه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Zakat is singled out because it was difficult for Moses' people, who especially loved worldly wealth; prayer is omitted because piety already encompasses every duty and avoidance of every prohibition.
rows.anchor: وتخصيص إيتاء الزكاة بالذكر مع اقتضاء التقوى له للتعريض لقوم موسى عليه السلام لأن ذلك كان شاقا عليهم لمزيد حبهم للدنيا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Belief in God's signs means believing continually in all the signs; repeating the relative pronoun emphasizes this completeness and hints at those who accept some signs but reject others, like Moses' people.
rows.anchor: والذين هم بآياتنا ( كلها كما يفيده الجمع المضاف يؤمنون

rows.speaker: شيخ الإسلام
rows.claim: The Shaykh suggests Moses' people had to atone for calf worship by killing themselves, and Moses' appeal for ease asked for good without hardship; God answered that their allotted mercy was joined to worldly punishment, while pure mercy would be written for later believers in Muhammad.
rows.anchor: جعلت توبتهم مشوبة بالعذاب الدنيوي ورحمتي وسعت كل شيء

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Reports from Ibn Abbas say Moses' prayer was made for those who believe in and follow Muhammad; another says Moses asked for something that God granted to Muhammad.
rows.anchor: وعن ابن عباس رضي الله تعالى عنهما دعاء موسى ربه سبحانه فجعل دعاءه لمن آمن بمحمد عليه الصلاة والسلام واتبعه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alusi judges the Shaykh's interpretation far-fetched.
rows.anchor: لكن لايخفى أن ماقرره هذا الشيخ بعيد

rows.speaker: صاحب الكشف
rows.claim: Al-Kashf says punishment applies to those who persist unrepentantly, while worldly mercy encompasses repentant and unrepentant alike; joining both mercies belongs to those prepared for it, so Moses' prayer benefits people who repent and remain steadfast.
rows.anchor: عذابي لغير التائبين إن شئت ورحمتي الدنيوية تعم التائب وغيره وأما الجمع بين الرحمتين فهو للمستعدين

rows.speaker: صاحب الكشف
rows.claim: On al-Kashf's reading, the answer encourages the people to continue repentance and righteous action, warns against returning to past misconduct, and transitions to the Prophet and the command to follow him.
rows.anchor: والغرض ترغيبهم على الثبات على التوبة والعمل الصالح

rows.speaker: الطيبي
rows.claim: Al-Tibi calls the reply a wise redirection: “My punishment” prepares the answer, while the actual answer is that God will write mercy for the qualified; Moses had asked especially for his own people, but mercy in this world is universal and the afterlife good requires further qualities.
rows.anchor: وقال العلامة الطيبي في توجيهه : إن هذا الجواب وارد على الأسلوب الحكيم

rows.speaker: الطيبي
rows.claim: Al-Tibi says “I will write it” grants what Moses requested in form but sets the qualifying conditions as multiple traits, not repentance alone.
rows.anchor: يعني أن الذي يوجب إختصاص الحسنتين معا هذه الصفات المتعددة لا التوبة المجردة

rows.speaker: الطيبي
rows.claim: Al-Tibi compares the answer to God's reply to Abraham about his descendants: the covenant does not reach wrongdoers; al-Hasan and Qatada also report that mercy covers righteous and wicked people in this world but belongs to the pious in the afterlife.
rows.anchor: ومن ذريتي قال لاينال عهدي الظالمين ) وأيد هذا التقرير بما روي عن الحسن وقتادة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alusi objects that Moses' prayer did not restrict divine mercy or ask to exclude anyone, so al-Tibi's charge of constricting what is expansive is misplaced.
rows.anchor: وما ذكره من حديث التحجر في القلب منه شيء فإن الظاهر أن ما في دعاء موسى عليه السلام ليس منه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses asked most emphatically for forgiveness, mercy, and good in both lives for himself and his people as repentant returners, not for them regardless of their state.
rows.anchor: إن موسى عليه السلام إنما طلب على أبلغ وجه المغفرة والرحمة الدنيوية والآخروية

rows.speaker: الزهري
rows.claim: Al-Zuhri reports that after the self-killing, God told Moses that those killed were alive and sustained with Him and that the survivors' repentance had been accepted, making Moses and Israel rejoice.
rows.anchor: فقد جاء عن الزهري أن الله تعالى أوحى إلى موسى بعد أن كان ما كان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Whether the repentance was through self-killing or another form, the promised acceptance of repentance supports the likelihood that the repentant people received afterlife good; many forgiven people receive it.
rows.anchor: وإن كانت غيرها فمن المعلوم أن التوبة تقبل بمقتضى الوعد المحتوم وخير من قبلت توبته في الآخرة كثير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their worldly good is also affirmed in God's reminder of His favor and preference for the Children of Israel.
rows.anchor: وأما خير الدنيا فقد نطقت الآيات بأن القوم غرقى فيه ويكفي في ذلك قوله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alusi offers another reading: God sees Moses' anxiety and first calms him by saying that punishment strikes only whom God wills, not necessarily the now-repentant people for whom Moses fears.
rows.anchor: أنه سبحانه لما رأى من موسى عليه السلام شدة القلق والاضطراب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because mercy encompasses everything, Moses' people surely remain within it; even the punished receive some mercy, since God does not punish them as severely as He could.
rows.anchor: ورحمتي وسعت كل شيء ) إنسانا كان أو غيره مطيعا كان أو غيره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God will write the fullest share of mercy for their later descendants at the end of time, who meet the stated qualities.
rows.anchor: بل إني سأرحمهم وأذهب عنهم ماأهمهم وأكتب الحظ الأوفر من رحمتي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The qualities are named to spur Moses' people to adopt or maintain them; the answer does not explicitly say their request is granted because that is more eloquent.
rows.anchor: ووصف أخلاقهم بما وصفوا به لإستنهاض همهم إلى الإتصاف بما يمكن إتصافهم به منه أو إلى الثبات عليه ولم يصرح في الجواب بحصول السؤال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alusi acknowledges flaws in this explanation but considers it better than many exegetical accounts and says transmitted reports are the best guide; if a hadith is sound, that is his position.
rows.anchor: إلا أنه أولى من كثير مما وقفنا عليه من كلام المفسرين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sīn in “I will write it” may signal emphasis or future time.
rows.anchor: والسين في ( سأكتبها ) يحتمل أن تكون للتأكيد ويحتمل أن تكون للاستقبال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse is attached to the preceding passage by an implied verb and binds Jews through a universal covenant, after their particular covenant and scriptural and rational arguments against imitation.
rows.anchor: وهو معطوف على ما قبل مسوق لإلزام اليهود بمقتضى الميثاق العام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some read the verse as a generalizing conclusion after the specific covenant at the mountain, showing the Jews' continuing transgression; Alusi says this is more apparent from the wording, especially if the general group is restricted to polytheists.
rows.anchor: وبعضهم جوز أن يكون تذييلا تعميما بعد التخصيص وإظهارا لتمادي هؤلاء اليهود في الغي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view takes the verse to establish a pre-world covenant with all humanity, the foundational basis of obligations, without coercion, and an answer to contemporary polytheists' excuses.
rows.anchor: إن الآية مسوقة لبيان أخذ ميثاق سابق من جميع الخلق مؤمنهم وكافرهم قبل هذه النشأة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage's placement among verses about Jews may be a digression linked by subject, but Alusi follows the majority of later exegetes in taking it as a universal covenant addressed to people generally.
rows.anchor: لكن الأول وهو الذي جرى عليه أكثر متأخري المفسرين أي واذكر لهم أو للناس إذ أخذ ربك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Children of Adam” means all people born generation after generation, believers and unbelievers, except those never born; Alusi rejects restricting it to Jewish ancestors who called Ezra God's son.
rows.anchor: المراد بهم الذين ولد لهم مؤمنين كانوا أو كفارا نسلا بعد نسل سوى من لم يولد له بسبب من الأسباب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Using “took” rather than “brought out” dignifies the covenant and its recipients, signals selection, supports the later question, and suits the language of covenant; “Lord” recalls the effects of lordship.
rows.anchor: وإيثار الأخذ على الإخراج للإيذان بشأن المأخوذ إذ ذاك لما فيه من الأنباء عن الاجتباء والاصطفاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some infer from the change of style around this verse that it is a digression; Alusi notes the different wording from the mountain-covenant passage and the following account of the man given signs.
rows.anchor: واستأنس بعضهم بمغايرة أسلوب هذا الكلام بما فيه من الالتفات لما قبله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “From their backs” is parsed as a partitive apposition to “Children of Adam” through repetition of the preposition; Abu al-Baqa instead treats it as an apposition of inclusion.
rows.anchor: من ظهورهم ) بدل من بني آدم بدل البعض من الكل بتكرير الجار

rows.speaker: أبو البقاء
rows.claim: Abu al-Baqa's inclusion-apposition analysis relates taking the descendants from the backs to taking Adam's descendants through their bodies and members; Alusi questions its rationale and prefers the partitive analysis.
rows.anchor: وإليه ذهب أبو البقاء وبينه بعضهم بأن بدل الاشتمال ما يكون بينه وبين المبدل منه ملابسة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Both occurrences of “from” indicate origin, further clarify the phrase by moving from general to specific, and may suggest the covenant was taken while people remained in their fathers' loins.
rows.anchor: في الموضعين ابتدائية وفيه مزيد تقرير لابتنائه على البيان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The object “their descendants” is delayed because it contains a pronoun referring back to the object and because delaying it preserves its primacy and creates anticipation.
rows.anchor: ذريتهم ( مفعول ( أخذ ) أخر عن المفعول بواسطة الجار

rows.speaker: نافع وأبو عمر وابن عامر ويعقوب
rows.claim: These readers recite the word as a plural; it means their children generally, while interpreters who restrict the verse to Jewish ancestors restrict it to their descendants, a limitation Alusi rejects.
rows.anchor: وقرأ نافع وأبو عمر وابن عامر ويعقوب ( ذرياتهم ) والمراد أولادهم على العموم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The objection that all people are both Children of Adam and their descendants is resolved by taking the verse as the ordered emergence of branches from roots through birth; no restriction to Jews is needed.
rows.anchor: والإشكال المشهور هو أن كل الناس يصدق عليه بنو آدم وذريته فيتحد المخرج والمخرج منه مدفوع بظهور أن المراد إخراج الفروع من الأصول
